body.objective: Students will be able to analyze human impact on an Alberta environment.

body.hook: Alberta's landscapes provide energy, food, timber, homes and recreation, and each use changes the land. Understanding those impacts is the first step to making better decisions about how we share it.

study.title: People and the Land
study.question: How do human activities affect Alberta environments?
study.passage:
Land-use case cards (written for this lesson; groups take one each):
1. Agriculture: crops and ranching feed people and support the economy. Much native grassland has been ploughed; ranching on native grass can help keep grassland intact.
2. Energy development: oil, gas, wind and solar provide energy and jobs. Impacts can include land disturbance, linear features (roads, seismic lines, pipelines), and water use; companies are required to reclaim land.
3. Forestry: provides wood and jobs; clear-cuts change habitat; replanting is required.
4. Urban growth: housing and services for growing cities; pavement increases runoff; green spaces and parks help.
5. Recreation: parks and trails bring health and tourism; heavy use can erode trails and disturb wildlife.
Analysis: for your case, make a T-chart of benefits and impacts on land, water, air and wildlife. Identify one mitigation (e.g. wildlife crossings, reclamation, riparian buffers, trail maintenance).
Share: each group presents in 2 minutes; class looks for common impacts (like fragmentation).
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Analyze effects on land, water, air and wildlife
discussion: What impacts appeared in more than one land use?
Which benefits are most important to Albertans?
study.product: Analyze one Alberta land use with benefits, impacts and two mitigations, and present it to the class.

body.objective: Students will be able to learn Indigenous perspectives on land relationships.

body.hook: For thousands of years, Indigenous peoples have lived in relationship with the lands now called Alberta, building deep knowledge of plants, animals, seasons and fire. That knowledge offers important ways of thinking about how we care for the land today.

vocabulary.definition: Knowledge about the environment built by Indigenous peoples over many generations.
Giving back; caring for the land that cares for us.
A connection with responsibilities on both sides.
The planned use of fire by Indigenous peoples to care for land.

Respectful ways of asking for and receiving teachings.

study.title: Learning From the Land
study.question: What can Indigenous perspectives teach us about caring for the land?
study.passage:
Learning guide (written for this lesson; teachings vary between nations, and local knowledge keepers should be invited following school protocols):
Common themes shared by many Indigenous nations: land as a relative, not just a resource; responsibilities to future generations; reciprocity (take only what you need, give thanks, give back); everything is connected.
Traditional ecological knowledge examples: knowing when and where plants and animals can be harvested sustainably; seasonal rounds (moving with the seasons); cultural burning used by many nations to renew grasslands and reduce fuel; detailed knowledge of medicinal plants such as sweetgrass and sage.
Today: Indigenous Guardians programs employ community members to monitor and care for lands; parks increasingly co-manage with Indigenous nations.
Activities: 1. Listen to a local knowledge keeper or a teacher-selected video from an Indigenous organization. 2. Note key teachings and questions. 3. Compare: how is "land as a relative" different from "land as a resource"? 4. Connect: link one teaching to something you learned in Outdoor Ed (e.g. reciprocity and Leave No Trace).
Respect: Indigenous knowledge belongs to communities; share teachings accurately and credit where they came from.
study.source: Summary written for this lesson; specific teachings should come from local Indigenous knowledge keepers.

body.objective: Students will be able to compare perspectives on land use.
body.iCan: I can compare perspectives on land use.
successCriteria: I can identify stakeholders in a land-use decision
I can explain different perspectives and the values behind them
I can propose a decision that balances perspectives
body.hook: A proposed project near a river: a rancher, a First Nation, a mining company, a town council and a birdwatchers' club all see the same land differently. Good decisions start with understanding every perspective.

vocabulary.definition: A person or group affected by or interested in a decision.
A point of view shaped by values and experiences.
Giving up one benefit to gain another.
Asking affected people for input before deciding.
A solution where each side gives something up.

study.title: Many Views, One Land
study.question: How do different perspectives shape land-use decisions?
study.passage:
Role-play scenario (fictional, written for this lesson): "Willow Creek Valley": a company proposes a gravel pit beside Willow Creek near a small town. Gravel is needed for roads and construction.
Stakeholder roles: 1. Gravel company: jobs, local supply, lower road-building costs; plans to reclaim the site in 20 years. 2. Local First Nation: the valley holds cultural sites and medicine plants; wants to be consulted and protect the creek. 3. Rancher: worried about dust, noise and creek water for cattle; might benefit from road upgrades. 4. Town council: needs jobs and tax revenue; also hears residents' concerns. 5. Conservation group: creek has trout and is a bird migration stopover; wants riparian protection. 6. Residents: concerned about truck traffic past the school.
Steps: 1. Read your role card; list your values and concerns. 2. Town hall: each stakeholder speaks for 1 minute. 3. Map common ground and conflicts. 4. In mixed groups, propose a decision: approve, reject or approve with conditions (e.g. setback from creek, truck routes, consultation agreement, reclamation bond). 5. Explain the trade-offs.
study.source: Original fictional scenario written for this lesson.
steps: Propose a balanced decision with trade-offs
discussion: Which perspective was hardest to understand?
What trade-offs did your group accept?
Why is consultation important before decisions?
study.product: Write a decision proposal for Willow Creek Valley that addresses at least four stakeholder perspectives and explains the trade-offs.

examples.problem: Suggest a condition to protect the creek.
examples.answer: A 100 m setback with no digging near the creek

examples.title: Trade-off
examples.problem: What is a trade-off of rejecting the pit?
examples.answer: Protects the valley but loses jobs and raises gravel costs
